questions.prompt: How do you read the current value of `const count = ref(0)` inside a <script> block?

options.text: count
count.value
count()
count.get()

questions.explanation: In JavaScript you access a ref's inner value through .value (count.value). In templates, top-level refs are auto-unwrapped so you write count.

questions.prompt: In a template, how do you display `const count = ref(0)`?

options.text: {{ count.value }}
{{ count }}
{{ ref(count) }}
{{ count() }}

questions.explanation: Templates automatically unwrap top-level refs, so {{ count }} shows the value — no .value needed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about reactive() are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It only works on objects, arrays, Map, and Set
Destructuring its properties keeps them reactive
Reassigning the whole object breaks reactivity
It provides deep reactivity for nested properties

questions.explanation: reactive works only on collection types, is deep, but breaks if you reassign the whole object. Destructuring its properties DISCONNECTS them from reactivity.

questions.prompt: To make a single number reactive, you should use ______(0) rather than reactive(0). (name the function)
questions.explanation: reactive only works on objects, so a primitive number must use ref(0).

questions.prompt: Why does a ref use a .value wrapper instead of just being a plain variable?

options.text: To make the code longer on purpose
So Vue can intercept reads and writes of .value to track and trigger reactive updates
Because JavaScript requires all variables to have a .value
To store the value on a server

questions.explanation: JavaScript can't detect access to a plain variable. Wrapping the value in an object lets Vue define a getter/setter on .value and observe every read and write.

questions.prompt: Which is the recommended default for reactive state, and why?

options.text: reactive, because it never needs .value
ref, because it holds any type, can be reassigned via .value, and survives being passed around
Plain variables, because they are simplest
It doesn't matter; they behave identically

questions.explanation: ref is the recommended default: it works for primitives and objects, can be reassigned through .value, and doesn't lose reactivity when destructured or passed around.
